_readme: Electron's safeStorage format on macOS, which is Chromium's OSCrypt:
"v10" ++ AES-128-CBC( PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1(password, "saltysalt", 1003, 16) )
with an IV of sixteen spaces and PKCS#7 padding. Unlike the vault's own
envelope there is no nonce, so a given password and string always wrap to
the same bytes — which is why this fixture can pin them.
What it proves: that src-tauri/src/safe_storage.rs is a correct
implementation of that scheme. The blobs were produced by a Node script
written from the numbers above and sharing no code with the Rust, so the
two agreeing is evidence and not a tautology.
What it does NOT prove: that Electron's safeStorage actually implements
this scheme, or that it reads the keychain item this backend reads. No
fixture can — it takes Electron and a login keychain. That check exists,
as tools/safe-storage-vectors.js and the ignored test beside it in
src-tauri/src/safe_storage.rs; run them together when a machine with both
is at hand.
If they disagree, a vault sealed under one backend asks for its recovery
key under the other. That fails safe — nothing is lost, the reader is
asked for what they wrote down — but nothing about it announces itself.
The passwords here are test values. The real one is sixteen random bytes
Chromium generated and keeps in the login keychain, and it is never
written down anywhere — not here, and not in vault-keys.json.
Run: cargo test (Rust). The TypeScript has no port of this to hold; the
Electron side calls safeStorage rather than implementing it.
